paras: The killing of Jeff Hill was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable J. M. Senac in Justice Langlois' court at New Iberia, Louisiana, on a Monday in June 1881, most likely June 6, while Hill was being tried on his wife's complaint that he had beaten her. Senac surrendered and was released on $500 bail, and a guard was placed at the jail after a rumor that Black residents meant to lynch him.

According to the Iberia Star, a "colored woman" swore an affidavit before Justice Langlois accusing her husband, Jeff Hill, of maltreating her, and a warrant was issued for assault and battery with intent to kill. Constable Senac arrested Hill and brought him before the justice the same day.

During the hearing, the local papers said, Hill grew angry at his wife's testimony and threatened her or tried to assault her again. The Star reported that Hill cursed when the justice warned him he would be jailed, declared that no judge or constable would jail him, and advanced on the two officers. Senac then drew his pistol and fired, and the ball struck Hill in the right side, killing him at once.

Senac gave himself up and stayed in jail until a preliminary examination before Judge Fontelieu, who released him on $500 bail to appear at the next term of the District Court. The Sugar Bowl reported that on Monday and Tuesday it was rumored that "some negroes" meant to take Senac from jail and lynch him, but a strong guard was placed around the jail and no attempt was made. No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial of Senac appears in the coverage.

Outside Louisiana, a New Orleans dispatch ran in the Chicago Daily Tribune on June 17 under the heading "SHOT DEAD BY AN OFFICER" among other crime briefs. In Louisiana the Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian reprinted the New Iberia Sugar Bowl's account on June 21 and again on June 25, and the Iberia Star's account on June 30; the St. Landry Democrat carried the Star's version on July 2. All three versions described Hill as violent and the constable as answering a threat, and none questioned Senac's use of his gun.

The accounts differ on what Hill did before he was shot: the wire said he knocked down and kicked his wife, knocked over the judge and attacked the constable with a razor, the Sugar Bowl that he made "a motion as if to draw a weapon," and the Star mentioned no weapon at all. The wire, dated June 10, placed the shooting on Monday, June 6, while the Star of June 18 called it "Last Monday"; the earlier dateline favors June 6.

reader.title: Killing of Jeff Hill
bases: A single constable shot a Black prisoner in a justice's court while ordered to take him to jail, with no mob involved in the killing (A1, A2, A4).

A New Orleans wire dispatch and two separate New Iberia weeklies (the Sugar Bowl and the Star, both quoted in Baton Rouge) agree that Constable Senac shot and killed Jeff Hill in court during a wife-beating case (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: New Orleans wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Hill knocked down and kicked his wife in court, knocked over Judge Langlois and attacked the constable with a razor, and the constable shot him 'dead in his tracks'.

accounts.label: New Iberia Sugar Bowl
accounts.gist: Hill attempted a second assault on his wife during the trial, resisted being taken to jail and made 'a motion as if to draw a weapon' before Senac fired.

accounts.label: Iberia Star
accounts.gist: Hill threatened his wife, cursed, said no judge or constable would jail him and advanced on the two officers 'with determined vengeance' when Senac fired; no weapon is mentioned.

framing.detail: The local weeklies describe Hill's 'passion' and threats and present the shooting as the officer's answer, with no comment on Senac's conduct.
The Chicago Tribune ran the wire as a brief headed 'SHOT DEAD BY AN OFFICER.' among other shootings, repeating the officer-side version with a razor.
